titel: Costs of a securities order in the US
kurz: With zero commissions, almost all trading costs are contained in the price, and they can be measured to the cent; the largest cost block, though, is often the tax.

bloecke.md:
A securities order causes two kinds of costs. The explicit costs appear on the trade confirmation: commission, the small regulatory fees on sales, fees for foreign trades and currency conversion. For online trades in US stocks and ETFs, the commission is usually $0. The implicit costs, by contrast, appear nowhere. They are not charged as a fee and arise from a worse price. For almost all private investors in the US, they make up the larger part.

The difference has practical consequences. Explicit costs are known before the order is sent and can be reduced by choosing a broker. Implicit costs only arise at the moment of execution. They depend on the security, the time of day, the size of your own order and the way the order is routed, and they do not appear in any statement. Investors who want to know them have to measure them themselves.

## Measuring the bid-ask spread

The bid-ask spread is the gap between the highest buy order (bid) and the lowest sell order (ask). An immediate purchase is executed at the ask price, an immediate sale at the bid price. The fair reference price lies in between. A single trade therefore costs half the [[Spread|spread]]. The full spread is only incurred on a round trip, that is on a purchase and a later sale.

bloecke.formel: Spread in basis points = (Ask − Bid) / Mid × 10,000
bloecke.erklaerung: A basis point is one hundredth of a per cent. The spread in basis points makes costs comparable across securities and order sizes. A single order bears half of it.
variablen: Lowest selling price in the order book
Highest buying price in the order book
Average of the two. Nobody pays this price, yet everything is measured against it
bloecke.beispiel: With a bid of 99.98 and an ask of 100.02, the result is (0.04 / 100.00) × 10,000 = 4 basis points. A purchase costs 2 basis points of this, that is $1 per $5,000 of order volume.

bloecke.md:
However, the quoted spread is only an offer for a certain volume. Only the [[Effective spread|effective spread]] shows the costs actually incurred on an order. It is twice the distance between the execution price and the mid price at the moment the order was received, and is therefore directly comparable with the quoted spread. The order itself costs the single distance, that is half the effective spread. In the US, many retail orders are filled slightly inside the quoted spread by wholesale market makers (price improvement), so the effective spread can be smaller than the quoted one. This gives a measurement method that any investor can use. Before sending the order, you note the bid and ask prices and compare them with the price on the trade confirmation after execution. The difference gives the implicit costs of this order to the cent.

Market centers publish monthly statistics on effective spreads and price improvement under SEC Rule 605, and brokers publish quarterly order routing reports under Rule 606. In 2024, the SEC adopted amendments that extend the execution quality reports to larger brokers and make them easier to compare. For the largest US index ETFs, the quoted spread during the regular session is often just one cent, a fraction of a basis point at their share prices. Outside the regular session and for smaller ETFs, it is considerably wider.

## Order size and market impact

The best spread only applies to the number of shares offered at the best price. Anything beyond that is executed at worse prices further down the order book. Most brokers show only the best bid and offer (Level I); depth data (Level II) shows further price levels. What remains invisible are hidden and midpoint orders on the exchanges and the liquidity of dark pools and wholesale market makers. For a large ETF with deep liquidity at every level, this does not matter for the order sizes of private investors, but for a small cap it does.

bloecke.titel: Ask side of a small cap in a model order book, mid between bid and ask at $24.77

bloecke.md:
A market order for 1,200 shares is executed with 300 shares at 24.80, 400 at 24.86 and 500 at $24.94. The trade confirmation shows $29,854, and the average price is 24.88. Compared with the mid of 24.77, that is $130 more. Of this, $36 is due to half the spread and $94 to [[Market impact|market impact]], that is the price movement caused by your own order volume. The commission of $0 changes nothing about this.

Only a limit helps against market impact. A limit order at 24.82 is executed at the first level, and the rest waits. In the process, 900 shares can remain open while the price moves away from the limit. These opportunity costs of not trading are real. Unlike market impact, however, they are not systematically negative, because the price can also move towards the limit.

bloecke.md:
## Time of day as a cost factor

A market maker quotes prices and takes on a risk in doing so. It does not know whether the other side is better informed, and it must be able to hedge its position. The less successful it is at this, the wider it sets the spread. This explains how spreads develop over the course of the day. The regular session runs from 9:30 to 16:00 Eastern Time. Spreads are typically widest in the first minutes after the open, when prices are still being found, and narrower during the rest of the session. Pre-market and after-hours trading take place with far fewer participants.

For an ETF with foreign shares, the markets for the holdings close during the US day: Asian exchanges before the US open, European exchanges around midday Eastern Time. The [[iNAV]] is then based on last prices from closed markets, and the market maker demands a wider spread for this uncertainty. Such ETFs are therefore often cheapest to trade in the morning, while European exchanges are still open.

Some brokers now offer trading in US stocks and ETFs almost around the clock on weekdays, through alternative trading systems. Outside the regular session, few participants trade, the exchanges' order books are closed or thin, and there is no NBBO from a full market against which the trade confirmation could be checked. The market maker bears the news risk until the next open and is paid for it through the price, that is implicit costs that do not appear on any trade confirmation.

## Costs of currency conversion

A foreign share can be bought as an [[American depositary receipt (ADR)|ADR]] in dollars on a US exchange, as an ordinary share over the counter in the US, or in local currency on its home exchange. The currency risk is the same in all cases, because the company's value is generated in its own currency, regardless of the currency in which the price is displayed. The routes differ in who does the conversion and how visible it is.

With an ADR, the market maker and the depositary bank handle the conversion and include their margin in the price and in the dividend payment. Depositary banks also charge ADR fees, typically a few cents per share a year, which are deducted from dividends or charged to the account. When buying on the home exchange, the broker charges a conversion fee, usually as a percentage of the transaction value, on the purchase, on the sale and on every dividend. The fee is only visible in the second route. The first route is therefore not cheaper; its costs are just harder to check.

bloecke.titel: Payment for order flow and execution quality
bloecke.md: In the US, payment for order flow is legal. Most retail market orders in US stocks are executed by wholesale market makers that pay the broker for them and must fill at least at the NBBO. Whether the customer benefits or loses through price improvement can only be seen in the execution quality statistics under Rule 605 and in your own measurements, not in the commission. The EU banned these payments in 2024, with a transition period in Germany until 30 June 2026; in the US, the SEC's 2022 proposals for order-by-order auctions were not adopted.

## Foreign withholding tax on dividends

Foreign dividends are taxed twice before they reach a US investor. First, the source country, that is the country where the company is domiciled, withholds tax. Under most US tax treaties, the rate on dividends to US residents is limited to 15%. The US then taxes the full gross dividend, for qualified dividends at 0%, 15% or 20%. To avoid double taxation, you can claim a **foreign tax credit** for the foreign tax against your US tax on that income. However, only the tax actually owed under the treaty is creditable; anything withheld above it must be reclaimed from the source country.

bloecke.titel: From a $100 gross dividend on a foreign share to the net amount
bloecke.unter: Calculated for a qualified dividend in the 15% bracket, treaty withholding of 15% and the foreign tax credit, in a taxable account, excluding state tax.

schritte.name: US tax 15% on the gross dividend

bloecke.md: The calculation has a reassuring result. A US dividend of $100 in the same bracket also leaves $85 after tax. A foreign withholding tax of 15% is therefore not a disadvantage as long as the credit can be used. A disadvantage only arises from withholding above the treaty rate, from holding foreign shares in an IRA or 401(k), where no credit is possible, and in years without US tax on the dividend.

bloecke.md: Withholding tax above the treaty rate can only be reclaimed by application in the source country, which takes forms, certificates of US residence and often months. This is why the structure of a fund also matters. A US-domiciled international ETF pays the foreign taxes itself and, if more than half of its assets are foreign shares, can pass the credit through to you; it then appears on Form 1099-DIV. Funds domiciled in Ireland or Luxembourg are not an alternative for US persons, because they are treated as passive foreign investment companies (PFICs). The effect of withholding tax on the fund shows up in the [[Tracking difference|tracking difference]], never in the expense ratio.

bloecke.titel: Withholding tax in an IRA and in the 0% bracket
bloecke.md:
In an IRA or 401(k), no foreign tax credit is possible. A gross dividend of $100 from a Dutch share therefore becomes $85 permanently. The same applies to a US-domiciled international fund held in a retirement account: the credit it passes through is lost. For investors with both account types, foreign shares and international funds therefore tend to belong in the taxable account, as long as this fits the overall asset allocation.

In the 0% bracket for qualified dividends, there is no US tax against which the credit could be offset. If you file Form 1116, the unused credit can be carried back one year and forward ten years. If you use the simplified election instead, which allows up to $300 of foreign tax ($600 for joint returns) to be claimed without Form 1116, there is no carryover.

## Costs of rebalancing

A portfolio of $100,000 contains 70% equities and 30% bonds. In one year, equities return 15% and bonds 3%. Afterwards, the equity portion stands at $80,500 and the bond portion at $30,900, a total of $111,400. The target allocation requires $77,980 in equities. So equities worth $2,520 have to be sold and bonds bought for the same amount.

The transaction costs consist of a $0 commission and half the spread of 0.02% on $2,520 for each of the two trades. Together that comes to around $0.50.

For the tax, it is assumed that 40% of the sale proceeds are a long-term capital gain, that is $1,008. At the federal rate of 15%, that results in $151.20 in tax; above the thresholds for the 3.8% net investment income tax it would be $189.50, and many states add their own tax.

The tax is therefore about three hundred times the trading costs. When rebalancing, a fee comparison only reduces the smaller of the two cost blocks.

If, on the other hand, the investor's taxable income were within the 0% bracket for long-term gains, the tax would be zero. And if the same rebalancing took place in an IRA or 401(k), there would be no tax at all at that moment. The same rebalancing therefore costs between $0.50 and $190, depending on the account and the rest of the income in the year.

As long as you keep paying in, the target allocation can be restored via the next contributions: [[Cash flow rebalancing|cash flow rebalancing]]. With a monthly contribution of $250, the $2,520 shortfall in the bond portion is made up after just over 14 contributions that go entirely into bonds instead of equities. Each contribution reduces the shortfall by only $175, because $75 of it belongs in bonds anyway according to the target allocation. The realised gain is zero. Dividends can also be directed into the underweight asset class instead of being reinvested automatically. If you have retirement accounts as well, rebalance there first, because trades inside them trigger no tax. With a large taxable portfolio and a small contribution, at some point this is no longer sufficient. Then selling makes more sense than letting the allocation deviate from the target permanently.

A position of $50,000 in a broad ETF in a taxable account contains $20,000 of unrealised long-term gains. A competing product has an expense ratio that is 0.05 percentage points lower. The switch therefore appears to be a pure cost optimisation.

- Federal tax due immediately: 20,000 × 15% = $3,000.
- Annual saving: 0.05% of around $50,000 = $25.
- In purely arithmetical terms, it takes around 120 years for the saving to offset the tax.

The calculation exaggerates, because the tax would have been due anyway on a later sale, unless the shares are held until death and the heirs receive a step-up in basis. Strictly speaking, at least the [[Tax deferral effect|tax deferral effect]] is lost, that is the return that the tax amount would have earned until the later sale. Even this effect is greater than $25 a year over any realistic investment horizon. The situation is different if the position shows a loss: then the switch realises a deductible loss. The wash sale rule applies if the new fund is substantially identical; a fund that tracks a different index is generally on the safe side, while for two funds on the same index the question has not been settled.

Four types of cost, in descending order of how often they are underestimated: the realised tax when rebalancing in a taxable account, market impact for thinly traded securities, half the spread at an unfavourable time of day and currency conversion on every single transaction. The commission comes fifth, is usually $0 and is still the figure that brokers feature in their advertising.

1. Before sending the order, note the bid and ask prices and the time. The mid between the two prices is the reference price.
2. After execution, compare the price on the trade confirmation with this mid: for a purchase, (Execution − Mid) / Mid × 10,000 gives the implicit costs in basis points; for a sale, (Mid − Execution) / Mid × 10,000 applies. A negative value means price improvement.
3. Add the explicit costs from the trade confirmation, also in basis points of the volume.
4. Repeat the measurement over ten orders and take the average, because some individual deviations also turn out in the investor's favour. Only the average shows whether the costs come from the broker or from your own trading habits.

mitnehmen: With zero commissions, almost all trading costs are implicit: they are contained in the price and appear on no trade confirmation.
A trade costs half the spread, and any quantity beyond the best price level causes additional market impact; Rule 605 and Rule 606 reports show execution quality and routing.
Which type of cost predominates depends on the combination of order size, liquidity and time of day, not on the commission.
Foreign withholding tax up to the treaty rate can be offset with the foreign tax credit in a taxable account; in an IRA or 401(k), it is lost.
When rebalancing and when switching products in a taxable account, the realised tax is almost always the largest cost block, often by a factor of several hundred.

begriffe.text: Costs that are not charged as a fee and arise from a worse price. They include half the spread, market impact and delay costs. They do not appear in any fee statement.

Twice the distance between the execution price achieved and the mid between bid and ask at the moment the order is received. It measures the actual costs of a specific order, including any price improvement. The order itself bears half of it.

Price movement that an order triggers through its own volume when it uses up several price levels of the order book. Market impact grows disproportionately with order size and falls as liquidity rises.

Credit of foreign income tax, such as withholding tax on dividends, against US tax on the same income. Only the tax owed under the treaty is creditable. Claimed on Form 1116 or, up to $300 ($600 joint), directly on the return.
Restoring the target allocation by directing new contributions and dividends instead of selling. No gains are realised, so the largest cost block of rebalancing does not arise.
